sections.normalized_html: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle, as shown above. What is the area of the triangle if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 6] meters?
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/67eceeef1f2b8a0e5ee2c13da0e261ae]

An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle, as shown above. What is the area of the triangle if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 6] meters?

sections.normalized_html:
To find the area of the triangle, we draw radii from the center to each of the triangle’s vertices. This forms three identical isosceles triangles, each with a central angle of [MATH: 120^\circ,] as shown below.

Now, we take one of these isosceles triangles and draw an altitude from the center to the opposite side. This divides the triangle into two right triangles with angles [MATH: 30^\circ], [MATH: 60^\circ], and [MATH: 90^\circ.]

In each [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle:

  • Let the longer leg, which is opposite the [MATH: 60^\circ] angle, be [MATH: x.] Notice that it is half of our equilateral triangle's side length.

  • The hypotenuse is a radius of the circle and has a length [MATH: r = 6\:\text{m}.]

Next, in the [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle, the longer leg is [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}] times the hypotenuse:

[MATH: x|= r ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(2); = 6 ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(2); = 3sqrt(3)]

Therefore, our equilateral triangle's side length is [MATH: s = 2x = 2 \cdot 3 \sqrt{3} = 6 \sqrt{3} \: \text{m},] and the corresponding area of the triangle is [MATH: A|= (sqrt(3))/(4)s^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4)(6sqrt(3))^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4) ⋅ 108; = 27sqrt(3)m^{2}.]

  • The length of the hypotenuse is the radius [MATH: r] of the circle.

Finally, in a [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle, the longer leg is [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}] times the length of the hypotenuse:

Therefore, the radius of the circle is [MATH: 9 \sqrt{3} \: \text{ft}.]
